title: Australian politics live: federal Liberal senator Leah Blyth defects to One Nation

blocks.text: Federal Liberal senator Leah Blyth defects to One Nation
Leah Blyth, federal Liberal senator for South Australia, is defecting to One Nation and will become the party’s first upper-house member for the state, according to The Australian.
The move will cause recriminations in Coalition ranks because Blyth is a member of Angus Taylor’s shadow cabinet.
But she told the paper she no longer felt the Coalition was capable of opposing the Albanese government, which was “running the country into the ground”.
She said:

double quotation markI can no longer in good conscience tell Australians that the Liberal party can save this country. Australia is a country worth fighting for … I want our children to grow up proud of their country, with the freedom and opportunity to build a better life. One Nation has never shied away from confronting the uncomfortable truths facing our nation. They are the only party with the bold ideas needed to turn this country around.

blocks.text: Blyth defection shows disunity in Liberal party: Cabinet minister

Labor will get a good kick out of this story today, particularly after securing a few legislative wins with the help of the Greens this week. (Although I would say the wins were bigger for the Greens who got massive concessions out of the government on the digital duty of care, trusts, and private health insurance bills.)
Cabinet minister, Pat Conroy, doesn’t want to stick the knife in too hard though this morning, deferring the question to the Coalition.
But he says regardless of who defects where, the Liberals and One Nation “can’t govern without each other”.
He tells ABC News Breakfast:

double quotation markWe are facing at the next election clearly a Coalition and Liberals and One Nation with all the baggage that each of these parties brings to the table. They’re all anti-worker, they’re all extreme … this demonstrates, I think, more disunity in the Liberal Party under Angus Taylor.
Blyth ‘wasn’t a big contributor to the party room’: Jane Hume
The claws are OUT this morning.
The deputy Liberal leader, Jane Hume, has been stopped by journos on her way into Parliament House, and is clearly incensed by her Senate colleague Leah Blyth’s defection.
She, like Matt Canavan, says it’s a “disappointing decision”.

double quotation markThe fact that she feels that the Liberal party doesn’t reflect her views any more is a surprise to all of us. It’s certainly not something that she ever mentioned in the party room – but she wasn’t a big contributor to the party room.
Ouch.
Asked what her highlight of the year is, Hume says “unity” in the Liberal and National parties (notwithstanding the last 24 hours).

blocks.text: ‘Turncoat town’: Canavan takes a crack at Blyth and One Nation
Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, is pretty salty this morning – taking another crack at Leah Blyth over her defection from the Liberal party to One Nation.
He calls One Nation “turncoat town” by hoovering up defectors from other parties.
Speaking to journos in the press gallery corridor after his RN Breakfast interview, he doesn’t hold back:

double quotation markI think people see that as a defection, as a turncoat, and One Nation is becoming turncoat town right now, where they seem to be much more focused on taking people away from other political parties than changing the government, and therefore changing the policy and changing the direction of this country. I don’t buy Leah’s explanation that this is some grand policy principle. It instead just smacks of self-interest.
Krishani Dhanji
Good morning
Krishani Dhanji here with you for the final sitting day of the year, thanks to Martin Farrer.
Just when I thought this week couldn’t get any busier, Leah Blyth said “hold my beer”.
It’s going to be a cracker today – let’s get stuck in!
Blyth defection ‘smacks of self-interest’, Nationals leader says
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, has called Leah Blyth’s defection to One Nation “disappointing on a number of levels”.
Speaking to Radio National, Canavan said he thought he was friends with Blyth but that he had received no warning of her move.

double quotation markI always find it disappointing when someone leaves the party [that] they were elected under, particularly in the Senate, because I know as a senator, you’re not really elected in your own name, you’re elected as a party … And so it’s right that people feel a bit let down when someone[who is] elected by them ticking a party box changes parties after the election.
Speaking to Blyth’s reasoning that her values aligned more closely with One Nation, Canavan said the move “smacks of self-interest to me”.

double quotation markGood luck to her. Leah went to the election last year supporting net zero. She didn’t oppose the hate speech laws earlier this year, like we did – the Nationals. To turn around now a few months later and say … “my principles and policies are more aligned with One Nation,” I mean, give me a break.
Energy minister says geopolitical tension ‘infected’ Cop31 talks
Catie McLeod
The energy minister, Chris Bowen, has said the failed Cop31 negotiations he presided over were more strained than previous years.

Bowen, who served as president of negotiations at the talks in Turkey, was interviewed on the ABC’s 7.30 program last night about the conference, which did not result in consensus among the countries over a proposed “cover decision”, or an overarching agreement, for the conference.
Bowen told the ABC it was not unusual that the negotiations were difficult, but:

double quotation markThe difference this year was countries were a lot harder to budge from their position and frankly I felt a lot of geopolitical tension in the room on other issues infecting the conversation and making it so much harder to negotiate. I’ve been to five Cops, seen plenty of argy-bargy, but there was a lot more rigidness to the negotiations this year. We [Australia] have always supported transition away from fossil fuels. This year I had a slightly different job. Normally we go – I go – to Cops and argue for what should be in. This year my job, running the negotiation – was to find ... the strongest outcome that I could get 195 countries from Tuvalu to Saudi Arabia to agree [on].
As Guardian Australia previously reported, the biggest sticking point was whether the agreement would mention the need for the world to transition away from fossil fuels.
Tess Ikonomou
Labor and Coalition on cusp of gas deal
A federal scheme requiring Australia’s largest gas exporters to keep up to a fifth of their product for domestic use is likely to be announced, with Labor and the Coalition on the cusp of a deal.
The Albanese government and the opposition have been locked in negotiations to reach an agreement before parliament breaks for the year after Thursday.
Labor agreed to a carve-out from the policy for Western Australia, as the mining state already has its own reservation scheme.
But the Coalition has held out over a provision that will require gas companies to oversupply the market by 10%, arguing it will affect future investment.
The opposition has remained the government’s partner of choice for this policy, as the Greens demanded a 25% tax on gas exports in return for their support.
